subtitle: An April 1st reply proposing networks designed to be as slow and unreliable as possible.

tldr.problem: RFC 1216 poked fun at gigabit networking. This memo answers it as a mock research proposal for Ultra Low-Speed Networking (ULSNET).
tldr.mechanism: It pitches deliberately slow systems, such as tanks painted with 0 or 1, neutrino bursts sent through the Earth, and a 49-layer protocol stack, then lists more ways to reduce throughput.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st joke document with no technical requirements. It is Informational and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: A Mock Reply to RFC 1216
sections.content:
This is an April 1st joke document, dated 4/1/91. It is written as a memo from the fictional Consortium for Slow Commotion Research (CSCR), signed Vint Cerf/CSCR, and addressed to Poorer Richard and Professor Kynikos. It responds to the research program announcement in RFC 1216 on Ultra Low-Speed Networking (ULSNET).

The joke is played straight: the memo proposes a research program on low-speed, low-efficiency networks over "several eons". It argues that military users want ultra-robust systems and that a high degree of redundancy helps survivability, so very slow designs should interest DARPA and the Department of Defense.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a pretend letter from a pretend club. The club says it wants to build the slowest network ever, and it pretends this is a serious idea.

sections.title: The Proposed Slow Systems
sections.content:
The memo offers three designs. The land system uses M1A1 tanks, each labelled 0 or 1 in yellow paint four feet high on the turret. A forward observer in a tree or sand dune reads the binary values of a tank column and radios them to a mainframe, which voice-synthesizes the message and radios it back. Variants add reconnaissance satellites, long baseline interferometry and Landsat imagery, and the plan is to use SIMNET to simulate it all.

The undersea systems use the 16-inch guns of the Battleship Missouri to send a pulse-code modulated message through the Pacific Ocean to the Ames Research Center, with tests in the Persian Gulf in the summer of 1991. A "jam-resistant" alternative sends neutrino bursts from Batavia National Laboratory through the Earth to a site near Tierra del Fuego, Chile, at a maximum of about once every 20 seconds. Submarines would have to be scheduled to pass that site.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of wires, they would use painted tanks, big ship guns and invisible particles shot through the Earth. All of these are very slow ways to send a message.

sections.title: Ways to Reduce Throughput Further
sections.content:
Section 5 lists extra ways to make the network worse:

  • Anti-Huffman coding gives the most frequent symbol the longest code.
  • Minimum likelihood decoding picks the least likely interpretation of each symbol.
  • Firefly cryptography enciphers with one jar of fireflies and deciphers with another, so decipherment rarely succeeds.
  • Recursive self-encapsulation wraps each of the 7 OSI layers again, giving a 49-layer model.
  • Scaling swaps the tanks for shuttle launch vehicles.
  • Network management adopts a "Slow Network Management Protocol (SNMP)" with variables specified in Serbo-Croatian and computations in reverse-Polish.
  • Routing offers Mashed Potato Routing, which stores packets for long periods, and Airline Baggage Routing, which mislabels packets and avoids the real destination.
sections.plainLanguage: Each idea is a way to make things worse on purpose, like mailing a letter to the wrong town on purpose to make sure it takes forever.

sections.title: Closing, Notes and Security
sections.content: The memo ends by looking forward to "a protracted and fruitless discussion" as soon as the consortium can figure out how to transmit the proposal. A note says the Consortium was formed 3/27/91, and another says the Convection Machine is a trademark of a fictional company. The Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The pretend club says it cannot wait to talk about this, as soon as it works out how to send the message, which could take a while.

references.text: RFC 1216, "Gigabit Network Economics and Paradigm Shifts", the announcement this memo answers.
